name: GTx-027

lead: GTx-027 is an arylpropionamide-class SARM associated with GTx, Inc., investigated for breast cancer and stress urinary incontinence and occasionally listed by muscle-building readers among SARMs.

SARMs are designed to activate androgen receptors selectively. A 2017 mouse study examined whether tissue-selective SARMs increase pelvic floor muscle mass in ovariectomized mice. Its status is listed as Phase I, discontinued, or preclinical, and no human trial on muscle or appearance exists.

paras: It is not marketed, and no routine for physique use exists.
No human safety data are available in the sources reviewed. The SARM class is unapproved, banned by WADA, and linked in case reports to liver injury with recreational use.

angle.text: GTx-027 is a SARM explored for breast cancer and stress urinary incontinence, occasionally listed by muscle-building readers. It activates androgen receptors, and mouse work on SARMs reported more pelvic floor muscle mass. It is largely preclinical, with no data on physique.

lead: GTx-027 is an investigational, orally taken non-steroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) of the arylpropionamide class, developed by GTx, Inc. and a structural analogue of enobosarm (ostarine, GTx-024). SARMs are of interest to people who want muscle and strength gains, since androgen receptor activation in muscle and bone is how androgens build lean mass; in animals GTx-027 raised lean mass and muscle strength.[1][2][3]

GTx-027 was studied for breast cancer and stress urinary incontinence and was never marketed, and Wikipedia now lists it as an abandoned drug.[3] Sources differ on how far it progressed: one says it did not pass preclinical research and another says it reached Phase I before development stopped.[3] A 2017 mouse study examined whether the tissue-selective SARMs GTx-024 and GTx-027 restore pelvic floor muscle mass in ovariectomized mice, motivated by the lack of oral treatments for stress urinary incontinence.[2]
No physique or appearance trials exist. GTx-027 is not described as a common gray-market product; its sibling enobosarm is, and appears in anti-doping cases.[4][5]
infobox: Phase I, discontinued, or preclinical; sources differ[1][3]

paras: GTx-027 is a nonsteroidal arylpropionamide with the formula C18H14ClN3O3, a molar mass of about 355.78 g/mol and one chiral centre with (S) configuration, and it is an analogue of enobosarm (GTx-024, ostarine).[3] Enobosarm itself came from a family of arylpropionamides derived from the antiandrogen bicalutamide.[5]

GTx-027 is a nonsteroidal androgen receptor modulator with mixed effects, acting as both an agonist and an antagonist depending on tissue. In laboratory studies it slowed the growth of androgen receptor-expressing breast cancer cells, and in animal studies it increased pelvic floor muscle weight in ovariectomized female rodents and raised body weight, lean mass and muscle strength.[3]

In mouse models of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, GTx-027 and related compounds GTx-024 and GTx-026 were reported to increase body weight, lean mass and grip strength, and the researchers said these effects depended on the SARM mechanism.[3] Wikipedia notes the compound first appeared in the scientific literature by 2013, and a 2014 study examined related SARMs in triple-negative breast cancer.[3]

Tissue selectivity in SARMs is still debated. Proposed explanations include that SARMs are not substrates for 5-alpha-reductase and so are not amplified in tissues such as the prostate the way testosterone is converted to dihydrotestosterone, that differing balances of coactivators and corepressors in each tissue make SARMs agonists in muscle and bone but partial agonists or antagonists elsewhere, and non-genomic signalling through membrane receptors.[1]

Testosterone was discovered in 1935 and approved for medical use in 1939; anabolic steroids such as nandrolone (synthesised in 1950) improved on it but retained androgenic and liver effects, which motivated the search for non-steroidal alternatives modelled on selective estrogen receptor modulators.[1] In 1998 two groups independently developed the first non-steroidal SARMs: a University of Tennessee team that made an arylpropionamide, and Ligand Pharmaceuticals, which made a quinolone compound; the term SARM was introduced in 1999 and GTx later developed enobosarm, the most studied SARM.[1]

Investigators have studied SARMs for osteoporosis, cachexia, benign prostatic hyperplasia, stress urinary incontinence, breast cancer, muscular dystrophy, hypogonadism and male contraception, and no SARM has been approved by the FDA or the European Medicines Agency.[1]

The pelvic floor is rich in androgen receptors, and researchers proposed SARMs as possible oral therapy for stress urinary incontinence; a 2017 study in ovariectomized mice reported that GTx-024 and GTx-027 restored pelvic muscles to the weight seen in sham-operated animals, with a trend toward higher total lean mass that was not statistically significant.[2] The related SARM enobosarm did not meet its endpoint in a Phase II trial for stress urinary incontinence and was abandoned.[1][5]

For context, enobosarm in two phase 3 trials in cancer-related muscle wasting increased lean body mass by roughly 0.4 to 0.5 kg without improving stair-climb power, and in a phase 2 study in healthy elderly people increased lean mass by about 1.3 kg over placebo.[5]

Enobosarm was licensed by GTx from the University of Tennessee, partnered with Merck from 2007 to 2010, and later developed by Veru; a 2011 phase 2 trial in older adults showed gains in lean mass and physical function, and a 2018 phase 2 trial for stress urinary incontinence missed its primary endpoint.[5] The two phase 3 lung cancer trials reported in 2013 found lean mass gains of roughly 0.4 to 0.5 kg without improved strength, and breast cancer became the main focus.[5]

Wikipedia describes SARM adverse effects in trials as generally mild and infrequent, with no aromatisation into estrogen, but notes raised liver enzymes, lowered HDL cholesterol, dose-dependent suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and case reports of liver injury with recreational use; cardiovascular risk is unknown.[1] For enobosarm, reported effects include headache, fatigue, anaemia and nausea, and the FDA has warned that SARMs can cause serious harms including heart attack, stroke and liver damage.[5] No human safety data on GTx-027 specifically are available.[3]

SARMs are not FDA approved but are sold online, and athletes' use has led to positive tests across several sports bodies, according to a 2023 systematic review poster.[4] WADA has banned the class since 2008.[1][5] GTx-027 itself is not described as a common gray-market product.

WADA's ban dates from 2008 with a first adverse finding in 2010, and enobosarm and LGD-4033 are the most frequently detected SARMs; Wikipedia notes SARMs are sold online as research chemicals, that a study found most products advertised as SARMs were mislabelled, and that in Australia SARMs are Schedule 4 (prescription only).[1][5]
No studies found for GTx-027 in humans for appearance or muscle gain. The available research on its therapeutic areas is preclinical, such as the mouse pelvic-floor study.[2][3]

timeline.event: University of Tennessee and Ligand Pharmaceuticals teams independently develop the first non-steroidal SARMs.[1]
GTx partners with Merck on enobosarm.[5]
GTx-027 appears in the scientific literature.[3]
Mouse study reports GTx-024 and GTx-027 restore pelvic floor muscle mass.[2]
